title: The Sphere in the Cylinder: Archimedes, the King's Machines, and the Figures in the Dust
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Syracuse, a birth date reckoned backward
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No ancient source gives a birth year. The figure c. 287 BCE is modern arithmetic: John Tzetzes, writing in the twelfth century CE, says Archimedes died at seventy-five, and the death year 212 is secure. Month and day defaulted to 01-01. The birthplace neighborhood is not attested either; Ortygia is the customary placement of the old city.
stops.campa: No writer of his own century records the year Archimedes is born. The date stands on one line in John Tzetzes, a Byzantine scholar fourteen hundred years downstream, saying he died at seventy-five; subtract that from the sack of 212 and 287 falls out. Syracuse in that year is the largest Greek city in the world, a Corinthian foundation spread over an island and three mainland quarters, rich on grain, harbor dues, and the wars of Sicily. What house receives him is not recorded.
suggested_refs: John Tzetzes, Chiliades, the sole basis for the traditional lifespan of seventy-five years
sources: J. J. O'Connor and E. F. Robertson, 'Archimedes', MacTutor History of Mathematics, mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk
John Tzetzes, Chiliades, as cited there

stops.name: Syracuse, the father named in a damaged line
stops.date_confidence: attested as text, undated. The Sand-Reckoner names Pheidias; the reading 'Pheidias my father' is Blass's emendation of a corrupt manuscript passage. The date here orders the segment only and carries no authority.
stops.campa: In The Sand-Reckoner, Archimedes needs a figure for the size of the sun, and he lists where the available figures come from. Eudoxus gives one. Pheidias his father gives another: the sun is twelve times the moon. That is the whole of the paternal record, one ratio inside a working list, and the manuscript is torn at exactly that point, so that the words naming the father are a nineteenth-century editor's repair. Archimedes does not say Pheidias measured the sun. He then measures it himself, sighting along a ruler with two small cylinders on it, and reports the error his own eye introduces.
suggested_refs: The corrupt passage of The Sand-Reckoner naming Pheidias, and Blass's emendation
sources: Archimedes, The Sand-Reckoner, text and notes at ucolick.org/~laugh/reckoner.shtml

stops.name: Alexandria, the schooling nobody records
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No surviving ancient text places Archimedes in Egypt. The stop rests entirely on the inference from his correspondence with Mouseion scholars. Date is a conventional placement in his twenties and is not evidence.
stops.campa: Nothing in any surviving text says Archimedes crossed to Egypt. What survives is his address book. He writes to Conon of Samos, to Dositheus of Pelusium, to Eratosthenes of Cyrene, all of them men of the Mouseion in the Bruchion quarter, and he writes as a colleague inside one workshop, not as a provincial sending work up to a capital. From that, biographers ancient and modern conclude he studied at Alexandria among the successors of Euclid. The inference is fair, and it rests entirely on letters. No text records a crossing, and the Mouseion's ground has never been located by excavation.
suggested_refs: The dedicatory prefaces of On the Sphere and Cylinder, On Spirals, and The Method, the whole evidentiary basis for the Alexandrian years
sources: T. L. Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897), prefaces

stops.name: Alexandria, propositions sent to Conon of Samos
stops.date_confidence: attested as correspondence, undated. Conon's death is placed before c. 240 BCE. Whether the exchange required Archimedes' presence in Alexandria or was conducted entirely by letter from Syracuse is not established.
stops.campa: Conon of Samos is the reader Archimedes trusts with a hard result. He sends propositions east and waits for judgment on them. No work of Archimedes addressed to Conon survives; what survives is Archimedes writing about him afterward, in the past tense, to a third man. The loss is technical as well as personal. A proposition nobody competent can check is not yet a proof, and the number of people in the Greek world able to check these runs to perhaps three.
stops.quote: When I heard that Conon, who was my friend in his lifetime, was dead
stops.quote_source: Archimedes, preface to Quadrature of the Parabola, in T. L. Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897)
suggested_refs: The prefaces addressed to Dositheus, which preserve the record of the earlier Conon correspondence

stops.name: Syracuse, the false propositions and the men who claimed them
stops.date_confidence: attested from the preface to On Spirals; date approximate, keyed to Conon's death and defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: In the preface to On Spirals, Archimedes explains what he has been doing since Conon died. He had circulated results without their proofs. Certain mathematicians then announced those results as their own discoveries, having proved nothing. So he salted the batch: among the true propositions he sent out two that are false, so that anyone claiming to have proved everything would be caught claiming to have proved the impossible. He reports the trap in a letter to Dositheus of Pelusium, who receives from now on the finished treatises, proofs and all.
suggested_refs: The preface to On Spirals, addressed to Dositheus, in Heath's translation
sources: Archimedes, On Spirals, preface, in Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897)

stops.name: Alexandria, The Method sent to Eratosthenes
stops.date_confidence: attested as to recipient and content; undated. The text survives uniquely and incompletely in the Archimedes Palimpsest. Date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: To Eratosthenes, who runs the Library and has measured the earth, Archimedes sends the one work in which he explains how he actually finds things out. He weighs figures against each other on an imaginary balance, slicing a solid into indivisible sections and hanging them from a lever arm until the unknown volume declares itself. This, he says, is discovery, not demonstration; the geometrical proof still has to be built afterward. No other Greek mathematician sets down how he came to a result rather than how it is proved.
suggested_refs: The Method of Mechanical Theorems, surviving only in the erased undertext of the Archimedes Palimpsest
sources: Archimedes, The Method of Mechanical Theorems, preface

stops.name: Syracuse, the sand-grains counted for Gelon
stops.date_confidence: attested as to text and addressee; undated. Gelon, son of Hiero II, died before his father in 216 BCE, which is the only firm bound. Place of composition inferred from the royal address.
stops.campa: Addressing Gelon, son of the king, Archimedes takes up the common opinion that the sand cannot be numbered, and answers it by building a numbering system that runs past anything Greek notation can hold, in orders and periods stacked on the myriad of myriads. Then he needs a cosmos to fill. He takes the largest one on offer, the hypothesis of Aristarchus of Samos in which the earth runs around the sun and the sphere of the fixed stars is vast beyond proportion, and he fills that with sand. The count comes out finite. Gelon dies before his father, in 216 BCE.
suggested_refs: The Sand-Reckoner's summary of Aristarchus of Samos, the fullest surviving ancient statement of the heliocentric hypothesis

stops.name: Syracuse, kinsman and friend of Hiero II
stops.date_confidence: tradition. Plutarch, writing more than three centuries later, calls Archimedes a kinsman and friend of Hiero II; no degree of kinship is specified anywhere and the claim may be inference from the engineering work. Date is a placement inside Hiero's reign (270-215 BCE).
stops.campa: Hiero II holds Syracuse for fifty-four years by not fighting Rome, and the peace pays for engines. The king asks questions that have an object in them, a crown or a ship or a stretch of wall, and gets back a machine together with a proof of why the machine must work. Plutarch, three centuries downstream, calls Archimedes his kinsman and friend. In what degree no source says. Whether the kinship is real, or a later reader's explanation for why a king kept a geometer at hand, cannot be settled from what survives.
suggested_refs: The royal precinct at the tip of Ortygia, later the site of Castello Maniace
sources: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 14, livius.org, 'The Death of Archimedes'

stops.name: Syracuse, the loaded ship drawn by one man
stops.date_confidence: tradition. Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 14, written roughly three and a half centuries after the event. Plutarch names only 'the arsenal'; the placement at the small harbor rather than the Great Harbour is plausible reconstruction. Month arbitrary.
stops.campa: Archimedes tells the king that any given weight can be moved by any given force, and Hiero asks him to show it. He has a merchantman hauled out of the royal arsenal, freighted with cargo and with men aboard, and rigs a compound pulley to it. Then he sits at a distance and pulls the line by hand, without strain, and the ship comes over the ground as evenly as if she were already under way at sea. Plutarch is the only source, writing three and a half centuries later, and he names the place only as the arsenal.
stops.quote: with any given force it was possible to move any given weight
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 14.7, Perrin translation (Loeb), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The Porto Piccolo of Syracuse, the sheltered harbor identified with Hiero's arsenal

stops.name: Syracuse, a place to stand
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and the wording is unstable. Plutarch has 'another earth'; Pappus of Alexandria, c. 340 CE, gives the form closest to the modern epigram; Tzetzes gives a Doric version. No text of Archimedes contains any of them. Date is an ordering device attached to the pulley demonstration.
stops.campa: The boast attached to the demonstration outlives every proof he wrote. Plutarch's version is conditional and strange: if there were another world, and he could get to it, he could move this one. Pappus, six centuries after Archimedes, gives the imperative that everyone now quotes, and there is no fixed English wording for it because there is no fixed Greek one either. What the lever proposition actually says is drier and harder, and it is the reason the sentence can be said at all: the ratio of the weights is the inverse ratio of the distances, without limit, in either direction.
stops.quote: Give me a place to stand on, and I can move the earth
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Archimedes by Pappus of Alexandria, Collection Book VIII (ed. Hultsch, 1878, p. 1060); rendering from T. L. Heath, The Works of Archimedes (Dover 1953), p. xix
suggested_refs: Pappus of Alexandria, Collection Book VIII, the earliest source for the lever epigram
sources: Pappus, Collection VIII, ed. Hultsch, via math.nyu.edu/~crorres/Archimedes/Lever/LeverIntro.html

stops.name: Syracuse, the launching of the Syracusia
stops.date_confidence: attested by Athenaeus quoting Moschion, both writing long after the event; the date is a modern placement late in Hiero's reign. No ancient source fixes the building slip, so the coordinate is a generic Great Harbour shoreline point.
stops.campa: Hiero orders a ship on a scale nothing in the Greek world can dock: three decks, gardens, a gymnasium, a bath, a shrine of Aphrodite floored in agate, timber enough for sixty ordinary hulls, and the Corinthian Archias building her. Archimedes gives her a stone-throwing engine, and a screw in the bilge that lifts water out of the hold by turning, and then the problem of getting her off the stocks at all. He rigs a windlass, and the hull that six hundred men cannot shift comes down into the water under his hand and a few helpers.
suggested_refs: The Syracusia, described by Moschion and preserved only through Athenaeus

stops.name: Alexandria, the ship renamed Alexandris
stops.date_confidence: attested that the ship was given to 'King Ptolemy at Alexandria' and renamed Alexandris, with a cargo of grain. The identification of that Ptolemy as Ptolemy III Euergetes, and the date c. 240 BCE, are modern inference and not in Athenaeus.
stops.campa: The ship is too large for any harbor in Sicily. Hiero gives her away to the Ptolemy reigning in Egypt during a grain shortage, loaded with ninety thousand bushels of corn along with salt fish, wool, and other freight, and on arrival she is renamed Alexandris. Athenaeus does not say which Ptolemy; the third is a modern guess. The bilge screw goes with her, and it goes on being built after that, turning in Egyptian fields and Dutch polders and mine sumps. It is still manufactured today, which is true of no other machine attributed to him.
suggested_refs: The Archimedean screw, the only device of his in continuous use since antiquity

stops.name: Syracuse, the crown and the bath
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and single-source. Vitruvius, writing roughly two centuries later, is the only ancient authority for the whole episode; no Archimedean text mentions it. Date arbitrary within Hiero's reign.
stops.campa: Hiero has given a goldsmith gold for a votive crown and suspects silver in what came back, and the crown may not be damaged. Archimedes carries the problem to the baths, notices the water going over the rim as he lowers himself in, and understands that the overflow measures the body and not its weight. Vitruvius says he ran home naked shouting that he had found it. Galileo, eighteen centuries later, works through the arithmetic, decides the bath cannot give the precision a wreath-shaped crown demands, and writes La bilancetta to reconstruct what he thinks Archimedes actually did: a balance, a fine wire, and the weighing done in water.
stops.quote: he immediately followed it up, leapt out of the vessel in joy, and, returning home naked, cried out with a loud voice that he had found that of which he was in search, for he continued exclaiming, in Greek, heureka (I have found it out)
stops.quote_source: Vitruvius, De architectura IX, preface 10, translation via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Galileo Galilei, La bilancetta (1586), math.nyu.edu/Archimedes/Crown/bilancetta.html
Scientific American, 'Fact or Fiction: Archimedes Coined the Term Eureka in the Bath'

stops.name: Syracuse, the sphere inside the cylinder
stops.date_confidence: attested as text; undated. On the Sphere and Cylinder is addressed to Dositheus, which places it after Conon's death, c. 240 BCE. Day and month defaulted.
stops.campa: A sphere is set inside the cylinder that just contains it, and Archimedes proves that the sphere is two thirds of the cylinder in volume and two thirds of it in surface, the same fraction twice over, which no one had any reason to expect. He sends it to Dositheus in two books. Of everything he does, this is the result he says he wants kept: not the engines, not the pulley, not the numbering of the sand. Plutarch says he asked his kinsmen to set that figure over his grave with the ratio inscribed on it.
suggested_refs: On the Sphere and Cylinder, Books I and II, addressed to Dositheus of Pelusium
sources: Archimedes, On the Sphere and Cylinder, in Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897)
Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 17, on the request for the figure on his tomb

stops.name: Syracuse, the circle caught between two polygons
stops.date_confidence: attested as text; undated. Measurement of a Circle survives in an abridged and probably damaged form. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: He draws a regular polygon inside a circle and another outside it, and doubles the sides, and doubles them again, to ninety-six on each side of the curve. The circle is trapped between two numbers he can compute exactly. It is a method of squeezing rather than of solving, and later work on pi proceeds the same way for the next nineteen centuries. He does not claim to have found the ratio. He states where it must lie: greater than three and ten seventy-firsts, less than three and one seventh.
suggested_refs: Measurement of a Circle, the ninety-six-sided polygons
sources: Archimedes, Measurement of a Circle, in Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897)

stops.name: Syracuse, the spiral
stops.date_confidence: attested as text; undated, addressed to Dositheus and therefore after c. 240 BCE.
stops.campa: Take a point moving out along a ray at constant speed while the ray turns at constant speed, and the track it leaves is the curve that carries his name. Archimedes finds its tangent at any point and the area it sweeps in one turn, which is a third of the circle it fits inside. The construction mixes two motions, and Greek geometry is not supposed to be able to handle motion at all. He handles it, and hands the result to Dositheus with the salted false propositions still fresh in the preface.
suggested_refs: On Spirals, the tangent construction and the area of the first turn
sources: Archimedes, On Spirals, in Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897)

stops.name: Syracuse, the law of the lever set down as geometry
stops.date_confidence: attested as a work of the Archimedean corpus, but with a reservation: parts of Book I of On the Equilibrium of Planes show textual layering that raises authenticity questions among modern scholars. Undated; the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Magnitudes balance at distances inversely proportional to their weights. Archimedes does not discover this as a workshop rule, which any porter knows; he sets out to prove it from postulates, the way Euclid proves a triangle, and then builds on it the centers of gravity of triangles, parallelograms, and parabolic segments. Modern editors reading Book I find seams in the text, passages that look added or reworked, and the question of how much of it stands as he wrote it has not been settled.
suggested_refs: On the Equilibrium of Planes, Books I and II, and the modern debate over Book I's layering
sources: Archimedes, On the Equilibrium of Planes, in Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897)

stops.name: Syracuse, the bodies that float
stops.date_confidence: attested as text; undated. On Floating Bodies survives through the Archimedes Palimpsest and a medieval Latin translation. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He begins with a fluid that presses equally in all directions, and derives from it what a solid does when set in one: it settles until the weight of the fluid it pushes aside equals its own. Book II then asks a harder question, whether a floating paraboloid tipped from its position will right itself or turn over, and answers it case by case for different proportions. A shipwright would call that stability, and no other ancient writer sets it out as a theorem.
suggested_refs: On Floating Bodies, Books I and II, Book II surviving only in the Palimpsest
sources: Archimedes, On Floating Bodies, in Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897)

stops.name: Syracuse, the cattle of the sun
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The Cattle Problem, a Greek epigram in twenty-two couplets addressed to Eratosthenes, is attributed to Archimedes but survives outside his main manuscript tradition, and the attribution is not secure. Undated.
stops.campa: Twenty-two couplets of Greek verse, addressed to Eratosthenes, ask how many cattle of the Sun grazed in Sicily, in four colors, with the bulls and cows of each color bound to the others by ratios, and then two further conditions that turn the whole thing into a Pell equation. The smallest answer runs to two hundred and six thousand digits. The poem travels separately from his treatises and reaches print only in 1773. Whether Archimedes wrote it cannot be shown either way.
suggested_refs: The Cattle Problem, twenty-two couplets addressed to Eratosthenes
sources: Heath, The Works of Archimedes (1897), supplement

stops.name: Syracuse, the death of Hiero and the turn to Carthage
stops.date_confidence: attested by Livy and Polybius as to the sequence; the month of Hiero's death is not fixed and is defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Hiero II dies after fifty-four years, and the Roman alliance he kept through two wars dies with him. His grandson Hieronymus, fifteen years old, listens to the party that says Hannibal is winning and turns Syracuse toward Carthage. Rome has been fighting for its life in Italy since Cannae and cannot afford Sicily going over. The engines he built for a king who never used them against Rome stand on the walls of a city that has just changed sides. Archimedes is in his seventies.
suggested_refs: Livy, Ab urbe condita, Book 24, on the succession of Hieronymus

stops.name: Syracuse, Hieronymus killed and the legions sent
stops.date_confidence: attested by Livy Book 24 and Polybius Book 7 as to the events of 214 BCE; the month is not fixed here and is defaulted.
stops.campa: Hieronymus is assassinated after thirteen months. The factions that follow him tear at each other until Hippocrates and Epicydes, men of Carthaginian service, hold the city and commit it fully. Rome answers with two commanders, Marcus Claudius Marcellus by sea and Appius Claudius Pulcher by land, and an army that has taken walled cities before. Syracuse has the longest circuit of walls in the Greek world, seventeen miles of it running out along the Epipolae plateau, and a defender who has spent Hiero's peace fitting engines to every stretch of it. The Romans arrive expecting a siege measured in weeks.
suggested_refs: Livy, Ab urbe condita 24, and Polybius, Histories 7, on the factional collapse of 214

stops.name: Syracuse, Euryalus and the engines ranged by distance
stops.date_confidence: attested by Polybius Book 8, the earliest detailed narrative, written by a man born about a decade after Archimedes died. The siege proper runs from spring 213 to autumn 212; month approximate. The fortress coordinate is Castello Eurialo.
stops.campa: The western approach to Syracuse runs along the Epipolae plateau to the fortress at Euryalus, and Archimedes has spent Hiero's money arranging the defense by range. Long-throw catapults hit the columns while they are still far off. As the range closes, shorter engines take over, each calibrated to its own band, so that an attacker is never out of somebody's zone. At the wall itself there are loopholes cut a hand's breadth wide on the outside, with small scorpions behind them, shooting men who cannot see where the bolt came from.
suggested_refs: Castello Eurialo, the western anchor of the Epipolae defenses

stops.name: Syracuse, the sambucae and the ten-talent stones
stops.date_confidence: attested by Polybius 8.4-8.6; month approximate within the first season of the siege, 213 BCE. The coordinate is a shoreline point on the Great Harbour walls; Polybius does not give emplacements.
stops.campa: Marcellus lashes ships in pairs and raises between them a ladder-tower four feet wide and as tall as the wall, hoisted by pulleys, and the machine is called a sambuca for its likeness to a harp. Archimedes drops beams on it. Timbers swing out over the parapet on chains and release stones weighing as much as ten talents, and lead masses, straight down onto the raised ladders and the decks beneath them. Marcellus takes to joking that Archimedes uses his ships to ladle sea water, and pulls the fleet back out of range.
stops.quote: they did not reckon with the ability of Archimedes, or foresee that in some cases the genius of one man accomplishes much more than any number of hands
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 8.3.3 (older numbering 8.5.3), Paton translation (Loeb), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Polybius 8.4-8.6, the technical account of the harbour assault

stops.name: Syracuse, the iron hand on the sea wall
stops.date_confidence: attested by Polybius 8.6; the placement along the Achradina shoreline rather than elsewhere on the sea wall is not specified by him. Month approximate. The modern name 'Claw of Archimedes' is a later coinage.
stops.campa: A beam runs out over the wall like a crane arm, and from it hangs a chain ending in an iron hand. When a ship comes close under the wall the hand is dropped, grips the prow, and the far end of the beam is hauled down inside the fortification by a weight or a windlass. The bow rises; the ship stands on her stern; then the grip is released and she falls, and she either swamps or capsizes or is smashed against the rocks. Polybius, writing within a lifetime of the siege from the accounts of men who were there, describes what the machine did and not how it was made. How it was built is still argued.
suggested_refs: Polybius 8.6, the iron hand and its use against ships at the sea wall

stops.name: Syracuse, the landward wall against Appius Claudius
stops.date_confidence: attested by Polybius 8.7. Polybius treats land and sea defenses together and gives no coordinates for individual engines; the pin is a generic point on the Epipolae landward circuit. Month approximate.
stops.campa: Appius Claudius brings up screens and ladders against the landward side, where there is no sea to pull his equipment out of. The same graduated system meets him there: heavy shot at distance, lighter and faster engines as the columns close, and stones and beams dropped from directly above once men reach the foot of the wall. Polybius says the Romans could neither advance nor stand still, and that they came to fear a rope or a beam appearing over the parapet more than the men holding it.
suggested_refs: Polybius 8.7, on Appius Claudius' blindages and ladders

stops.name: Syracuse, the assault abandoned for a blockade
stops.date_confidence: attested by Polybius 8; he gives roughly eight months of failed assault before the shift to blockade. The month here is derived from that interval and is not itself in the source.
stops.campa: After about eight months the Romans stop trying to take Syracuse by assault and settle for starving it. Marcellus divides the work, blockading the harbor, cutting the land approaches, and turning his field army loose on the rest of Sicily to keep a Carthaginian relief force off the city. Two consular armies have been held off a city wall by the arrangements of one old man, and the sources on both sides say so without embarrassment. The blockade runs on into the following year.
stops.quote: Such a great and marvellous thing does the genius of one man show itself to be when properly applied to certain matters.
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories, Book 8, Paton translation (Loeb), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories 8, on the shift from assault to blockade

stops.name: Syracuse, the mirrors that the early sources do not mention
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a negative one. Polybius, Livy, and Plutarch, the three earliest and fullest narrators of the siege, contain no burning mirror. The legend appears in Lucian ambiguously in the second century CE and is developed by Anthemius of Tralles in the sixth, then by Zonaras and Tzetzes. Date is a placeholder inside the siege.
stops.campa: The most famous engine of the siege is missing from every account written near it. Polybius describes the catapults, the scorpions, the beams, and the iron hand; Livy and Plutarch follow him and add nothing burning. The mirrors that set Roman ships alight arrive centuries afterward, hinted at by Lucian, worked out as a technical proposition by Anthemius of Tralles in the sixth century, and then repeated as history by Zonaras and Tzetzes. Modern crews have tried it on beaches with bronze and plywood, with mixed and mostly discouraging results.
suggested_refs: Anthemius of Tralles, On Remarkable Mechanical Devices, the earliest technical treatment of burning mirrors
sources: Absence in Polybius, Histories 8; Livy, Ab urbe condita 24-25; Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 14-19
Later notices in Lucian, Anthemius of Tralles, Zonaras, and Tzetzes

stops.name: Syracuse, the Hexapylon taken during the festival
stops.date_confidence: attested by Livy 25.23-24, which names the festival of Diana and the unexpectedly low stretch of wall. The identification of the entry point with the Hexapylon is Livy's, but the precise wall segment is a modern topographic inference. Month approximate.
stops.campa: The wall is never beaten. A festival of Diana runs for three days inside a blockaded city with little food and a great deal of wine, and a Roman officer sent to negotiate a prisoner exchange has been counting courses of stone by eye on his way in and out. On the chosen night the ladders go up against a stretch nobody thought worth guarding, near the Hexapylon at the north end of the Epipolae circuit. The postern is forced from inside. By morning the outer quarters belong to Marcellus.
suggested_refs: The Hexapylon gate at the north of the Epipolae wall, near the modern Scala Greca

stops.name: Syracuse, Achradina falls quarter by quarter
stops.date_confidence: attested by Livy 25.25-31 as to the sequence, though the district-by-district reconstruction is Livy's own narrative, written some two centuries later. Month approximate.
stops.campa: The city does not fall in one night. Achradina and the island of Ortygia hold on behind their own walls while plague works through both armies in the marshy ground outside, killing the Carthaginian relief force and its general. What finally opens the last quarters is not an engine but a Spanish officer's bargain and a gate left unlocked. Marcellus, looking down over the whole of Syracuse before the plunder starts, is said by Plutarch to have wept for what was about to happen to it.
suggested_refs: Livy, Ab urbe condita 25.25-31, on the plague, the betrayals, and the final surrender

stops.name: Syracuse, the figures drawn in the dust
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the killing; the circumstances are contradictory across sources and are not resolved here. Livy 25.31 makes the soldier ignorant of who Archimedes was; the motif that Archimedes did not know the city had fallen belongs to Valerius Maximus. The exact street and house are not recorded anywhere. Day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He is bent over figures he has drawn in the dust while the sack goes on around him. Livy says the soldier who killed him did not know who he was, and puts the ignorance on the soldier, not on Archimedes. Valerius Maximus says he asked the intruder not to disturb this, meaning the diagram, and was cut down with his blood running across the lines. Plutarch will not choose between three versions: killed in anger for refusing to leave an unfinished problem, killed while asking for time to finish it, or killed by men who took his instruments for a box of gold.
stops.quote: he was by himself, working out some problem with the aid of a diagram
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 19.4, Perrin translation (Loeb), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: Livy 25.31, thelatinlibrary.com/livy/liv.25.shtml, for the Latin 'ab ignaro milite quis esset'
Valerius Maximus, Facta et dicta memorabilia 8.7 ext. 7

stops.name: Syracuse, Marcellus turns from the man who did it
stops.date_confidence: contested. Plutarch and Valerius Maximus record an order that Archimedes be spared; Livy 25.31 gives no such prior order, only that Marcellus took the death hard, saw to the burial, and protected the relatives. The contradiction is left standing. Day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Marcellus is told, and the sources agree on what he does next even where they disagree on what he had ordered beforehand. He treats the killer as a murderer. He turns from the man as from something polluted. He has Archimedes buried, and he sends for the surviving relatives and puts them under protection. Whether he had given a standing order to spare the geometer, as Valerius Maximus and Plutarch say, or whether that order is a later tidying of the story, Livy does not confirm; he mentions no order at all.
stops.quote: was afflicted at his death, and turned away from his slayer as from a polluted person
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 19.6, Perrin translation (Loeb), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: The three incompatible death narratives: Livy 25.31, Valerius Maximus 8.7 ext. 7, Plutarch, Marcellus 19

stops.name: Syracuse, the grave arranged by the enemy
stops.date_confidence: attested by Livy 25.31 that Marcellus arranged the burial; no ancient source records where. The coordinate is a placeholder inside the captured city and is not a findspot. Day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The burial is arranged by the general whose fleet he had been sinking for two years. No source says where the grave was dug, or who chose what went on it, or whether Archimedes had left instructions. Livy adds only that the relatives were sought out and put under protection. What is known is what stood above the grave a century and a half later: a small column carrying a sphere set inside a cylinder, with verses cut under it giving the ratio between them.
suggested_refs: Livy 25.31, on Marcellus arranging the burial and protecting the relatives

stops.name: Rome, the two spheres carried out of Syracuse
stops.date_confidence: attested by Cicero, De re publica 1, writing some hundred and fifty years later. Month approximate to the fall of the city. The Temple of Honos et Virtus outside the Porta Capena is the standard topographic identification for a structure that no longer exists, so the coordinate is approximate.
stops.campa: Out of a city stripped of everything portable, Marcellus takes for the public account almost nothing, and keeps for himself two devices. One is an ordinary celestial globe, which he dedicates in the Temple of Virtue outside the Porta Capena. The other he keeps at home: a hollow mechanism in which sun, moon, and the five planets each move at their own rate, so that the model's moon falls behind its sun by exactly as many turns as the real one does in the sky. Cicero reports it as still running in 166 BCE, in the house of that Marcellus' grandson.
suggested_refs: Cicero, De re publica 1, on the two Archimedean spheres and the demonstration by Gaius Sulpicius Gallus in 166 BCE
The Antikythera mechanism, evidence that geared planetary devices existed in the Hellenistic world

stops.name: Syracuse, the column above the briers
stops.date_confidence: attested by Cicero's own first-person account in Tusculan Disputations 5.64-66, written around 45 BCE about a discovery he places in his quaestorship of 75 BCE. The Latin reads 'ad portas Agragantinas', the Agrigentine gate on the western approach; the reading 'gate Achradinae' in Yonge's older English version is an error. The monument itself is lost and the site cannot be fixed today.
stops.campa: A hundred and thirty-seven years after the sack, the grave is under briers in the necropolis outside the Agrigentine gate, and the Syracusans tell the visiting Roman quaestor that no such tomb exists. Cicero has heard the verses that were carved on it and knows what to look for. He finds a small column standing just clear of the scrub, with a sphere and a cylinder cut on it, and has the brush cleared away. About half the inscription is still legible.
stops.quote: I observed a small column standing out a little above the briers, with the figure of a sphere and a cylinder upon it
stops.quote_source: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.65, C. D. Yonge translation, Project Gutenberg ebook 14988
suggested_refs: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.64-66, the only description of the monument by anyone who saw it
sources: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.64-66, Yonge translation, gutenberg.org/cache/epub/14988

stops.name: Syracuse, the tomb the guides show
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and flagged as a misidentification. The rock-cut columbarium in the Grotticelle necropolis is Roman-period and does not match Cicero's description. The date is a nominal placement for the Roman period of the monument, not an excavation date; it is not attested.
stops.campa: In the Grotticelle necropolis, off the Viale Teracati, a rock-cut chamber with a columbarium inside it is signposted as the Tomb of Archimedes and has been shown to visitors under that name for generations. It is Roman work, later than Archimedes, and it carries neither a column nor a sphere nor a cylinder nor a verse. Cicero saw the monument outside a gate on the western approach, on the far side of the city from this chamber. Where that column stood is not known, and no excavation has found it.
suggested_refs: The Tomba di Archimede, Grotticelle necropolis, Viale Teracati, Siracusa

stops.name: Constantinople, a scribe copies the treatises
stops.date_confidence: attested in outline by the Archimedes Palimpsest project: a Greek copy made at Constantinople around 950 CE, descending from a sixth-century compilation associated with Isidore of Miletus. The specific scriptorium is unidentified and the year is a round approximation. This stop is manuscript history, not Archimedes' travel.
stops.campa: Eleven hundred years after the sack, a scribe in Constantinople copies out a collection of Archimedes in Greek: the Equilibrium of Planes, the Floating Bodies, the Spirals, the Sphere and Cylinder, the Measurement of the Circle, the Stomachion, and the Method that was sent to Eratosthenes. His exemplar goes back to a sixth-century compilation associated with Isidore of Miletus, one of the builders of Hagia Sophia. For The Method and for Book II of the Floating Bodies, this copy will turn out to be the only one there is.
suggested_refs: The sixth-century Archimedean compilation associated with Isidore of Miletus

stops.name: A Byzantine monastery, the parchment scraped for a prayer book
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the year 1229, which was recovered from a colophon decoded only in 2002. The place is not known; the pin repeats the Constantinople coordinate as a placeholder and should not be read as a location. Manuscript history, not Archimedes' travel.
stops.campa: Parchment is expensive and the mathematics is not being read. The leaves are cut apart, turned ninety degrees, scraped down, folded, and written over with the liturgy of a euchologion, a Greek Orthodox prayer book. The old text does not vanish; it goes faint and sideways under the new one, ink ghosts running crosswise beneath the offices. A colophon gives the year the new book was finished, though nobody will be able to read that colophon until 2002.
suggested_refs: The euchologion colophon dating the overwriting to 1229, decoded in 2002

stops.name: Basel, the works come off a press
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year, place, printer and editor; the exact print-shop address is approximated to Basel's old-town printing district. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Johann Herwagen prints at Basel the Archimedis Syracusani philosophi ac geometrae excellentissimi opera, Greek text and Latin translation together, edited by Thomas Gechauff Venatorius. It does not contain The Method, which nobody knows exists, or the second book of the Floating Bodies. What it does contain is enough to put the Sphere and Cylinder, the spiral, the parabola, and the law of the lever into the hands of every mathematician in Europe who can afford a folio.
suggested_refs: Archimedis Syracusani philosophi ac geometrae excellentissimi opera (Basel: Herwagen, 1544), the editio princeps
sources: Wikipedia, 'Archimedes', section on manuscripts and editions

stops.name: Wolfenbuttel, Lessing finds the cattle epigram
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1773 publication by Gotthold Ephraim Lessing from a manuscript at the Herzog August Bibliothek. Month and day defaulted. Manuscript history, not Archimedes' travel.
stops.campa: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, librarian at the Herzog August Bibliothek, goes through the Greek manuscripts and prints a twenty-two-couplet poem about four colors of cattle grazing in Sicily, addressed to Eratosthenes and ascribed to Archimedes. The verse has travelled fifteen centuries entirely outside his manuscript tradition, in company nobody has traced, and whether it is his cannot be shown either way. Its conditions collapse into a Pell equation; its smallest solution is not computed until 1965, on a machine, and runs past two hundred thousand digits.
suggested_refs: The Wolfenbuttel manuscript of the Cattle Problem, published by Lessing in 1773
sources: MacTutor, 'Archimedes', on the Cattle Problem's discovery

stops.name: Jerusalem, a catalogue entry for an undertext
stops.date_confidence: attested: A. Papadopoulos-Kerameus catalogued the prayer book at the Metochion of the Holy Sepulchre library and noted the mathematical undertext in 1899. Month and day defaulted. Manuscript history, not Archimedes' travel.
stops.campa: The prayer book has reached the library of the Metochion of the Holy Sepulchre, and A. Papadopoulos-Kerameus, cataloguing the collection, records that this one carries an older mathematical text underneath. He transcribes a little of what he can make out and prints the fragment in the catalogue, correctly, without knowing whose sentences they are. The entry goes into the printed catalogue and sits there for seven years, on a library shelf in Jerusalem, before anyone who recognizes the mathematics reads it.
suggested_refs: Papadopoulos-Kerameus' Jerusalem Patriarchate catalogue entry of 1899

stops.name: Constantinople, Heiberg reads the ghost text
stops.date_confidence: attested that Johan Ludvig Heiberg examined and photographed the manuscript at Constantinople in 1906 and identified the Archimedean undertext including The Method. The month is approximate. Manuscript history, not Archimedes' travel.
stops.campa: Johan Ludvig Heiberg, who has already produced the standard critical edition of Archimedes, reads the Jerusalem catalogue, understands what the entry describes, and travels to Constantinople. He works at the Metochion with a magnifying glass and a camera, page by page, transcribing what he can and photographing the rest. Under the offices of the prayer book he finds Book II of the Floating Bodies, the Stomachion, and the letter to Eratosthenes explaining how Archimedes found his results before he proved them.
suggested_refs: Heiberg's 1906 photographs, the only record of some leaves before the manuscript's twentieth-century damage
J. L. Heiberg, Archimedis Opera Omnia, revised 1910-15

stops.name: New York, the palimpsest sold at Christie's
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date, place, and buyer's anonymity. The reported price differs between sources, roughly two million US dollars in most accounts and 2.2 million in one; the discrepancy is left standing. Manuscript history, not Archimedes' travel.
stops.campa: The book has been out of sight for most of a century, and it has been handled badly: mould, missing leaves, and four forged Byzantine gold-leaf miniatures painted over the parchment at some point to raise the price. The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem sues to stop the sale, claiming the manuscript was taken unlawfully from its library, and loses, chiefly on limitations grounds rather than on any finding about ownership. It goes to an anonymous buyer for about two million dollars.
suggested_refs: The Christie's sale of 29 October 1998, and the Patriarchate of Jerusalem's unsuccessful suit

stops.name: Baltimore, the imaging at the Walters
stops.date_confidence: attested: the buyer deposited the manuscript at the Walters Art Museum, where conservation and imaging ran from 1999 to 2008, with the public data release on 29 October 2008 and the two-volume scholarly edition in 2011. The date here marks the start of that work; month and day defaulted. Manuscript history, not Archimedes' travel.
stops.campa: The anonymous buyer deposits the book at the Walters Art Museum and pays for it to be taken apart and read. Conservators separate the leaves; imaging teams work them under ultraviolet and infrared and multispectral light, and take the pages under the forged gold miniatures to a synchrotron, where X-ray fluorescence picks up the iron in the original ink straight through the paint. The Method, which had existed in one copy, becomes legible to anyone who wants it. The data is released publicly in 2008 and the scholarly edition follows in 2011.
suggested_refs: The Archimedes Palimpsest Project's imaging data, released 29 October 2008
Reviel Netz and William Noel, eds., the two-volume Palimpsest edition (2011)
